newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel prepares secondary offering in Bank Leumi.
newsitem.headline: Israel prepares secondary offering in Bank Leumi.

text.p: The Israeli government is planning a secondary offering for 10 percent of Bank Leumi, probably in the first quarter of 1997, the government official in charge of bank privatisations said on Monday.

Meir Jacobson, managing director of M.I. Holdings, the government company charged with selling the state-owned banks, said he had sent a letter to Leumi management asking it to prepare information based on its 1996 results for the prospectus.
He would not say whether the offering would be in Israel or overseas or reveal any other details. "I'm not interested in providing details," he said.

Unconfirmed press reports say M.I. Holdings plans to offer American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) in New York and Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs) in London. Approximately 18 percent of Leumi is already traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

Leumi is the second bank the government plans to float early next year. Israel Discount Bank is already preparing a prospectus based on its results for the first nine months of 1996 and will probably be floated in February, Jacobson said.
He would not say whether Discount would be floated in Israel or overseas. "It's too early to comment on details," he told Reuter.
The government issued 14 percent, on a fully diluted basis, of the bank in Tel Aviv earlier this year, with much of the issue bought up by overseas investors.

The two public offerings appear to mark a new effort by the Israeli government to rekindle its moribund bank-privatisation programme. The government floated shares in Bank Hapoalim and Leumi in 1993 but since then the bank-sale programme has lost momentum, in large part due to the slump in the domestic equity market since 1994.

In addition, investors are concerned about the banks' exposure to kibbutz debt, the ramifications of a new bank reform that is forcing the banks to sell off non-bank assets and the slowing of the Israeli economy.

A plan to offer shares in United Mizrahi Bank earlier this year failed and Edmond Safra, the sole bidder in a tender for a controlling stake in Leumi, Israel's second-largest bank, dropped out last year.
Hapoalim is being tendered now, but one of the two bidders has already dropped out and the second group has yet to win approval from the central bank to make a formal bid.
